html:
This section talks about how culture, peers, and language allows humans to learn faster (discover strategies faster) and deeper each generation, culminating in the present "information age", then dives into the specific benefits and roles of language as a representational medium

Cover Kieran Egan’s cultural toolkits

Benefits of language as a representational medium

Language discretizes continuous spaces. Before you have a word for something, your representation of it may be fuzzy and gradient. Once labeled, it becomes a discrete, manipulable object. Is this seen in nominalization?

Besides its communicative benefits, language is effective because language is compressive and compositional. You can bind together many concepts into a structured chunk ("the failure mode is distribution shift + sloppy evaluation + motivated reasoning"), and that chunk can steer perception, memory retrieval, and action selection without re-deriving everything from first principles or storing many high-dimensional, redundant vectors (i.e without simulating every detail). Words become handles for high-dimensional bundles of (non-verbal) experience: saying "I’m procrastinating because the task is ill-defined" can immediately trigger an action template (define success criteria -> reduce scope -> first small step). This is like calling a library function instead of rewriting code or simulating: fast, reusable, and easier to inspect.

This means language serves as an efficient yet expressive medium for controlling mental simulations

Language also serves as a substrate for cross-modal integration; by 25, language becomes a common currency that links otherwise semi-separate "apps" (emotion, planning, social inference, memory search, moral norms). The developmental punchline is integration: language becomes the standardized API that lets these modules call each other reliably; more of cognition becomes addressable, inspectable, and cross-module composable via linguistic pointers.

How much did language (compressive, symbolic, mutually interpretable) and social interaction (parallel, collaborative, multi-generation) influence the structure of and accelerate our acquisition of robust, abstract world modeling?

Abstractions are largely inherited (although they of course must be constructed from the ground up and (in most cases) must be error-corrected online to reach full robustness)

"We emphasize that the language network works closely with, but is distinct from, both lower-level - perceptual and motor - mechanisms and higher-level systems of knowledge and reasoning. The perceptual and motor mechanisms process linguistic signals, but, in contrast to the language network, are sensitive only to these signals’ surface properties, not their meanings; the systems of knowledge and reasoning (such as the system that supports social reasoning) are sometimes engaged during language use but are not language-selective." 1

The precise relationship between language and human thought is hotly debated 2

Language as a modulator to cognitive and neurological systems; Situating language in higher-order cognition; The Language of Thought Hypothesis; A language of episodic thought?; Is language necessary for thought?

Benefits of language as a representational medium, especially relative to visuospatial

The system definitely recruits and combines different kinds of representations for specific tasks

Is it fair to say that language serves primarily as a compressive interface/API for the self and other agents (expressive/communicative) and system of representational priors (the structure of language informs the structure of non-verbal representations/networks 8, 9) for the brain?

Relate to working memory model

Overall, however, visuospatial representations are likely more central and more fundamental to human thought, especially when you consider that visuo-spatial (and sensorimotor) representations serve as a necessary foundation from which linguistic representations are derived.

Really drill into this

Language as the operating system and controller

The "pointer" architecture

Childhood (The Label): The word "force" is just a label associated with pushing a toy. It’s a direct associative map.

Adulthood (The Handle): The word "force" becomes a low-dimensional "handle" that allows the brain to manipulate a high-dimensional sensorimotor simulation.

The Mechanism: When a 20-year-old engineer thinks "torque," they aren’t just retrieving a dictionary definition. The word triggers a compressed, non-linguistic simulation of rotational physics. The word is the address in memory; the "meaning" is the sensorimotor state it points to.

Developmental Shift: The 12-25 window is when the brain learns to trust the pointers enough to perform operations on them directly (algebraic manipulation of concepts) without having to fully unpack the sensorimotor simulation at every single step. This is cognitive efficiency.

Language as the control system

The Base Layer: The brain is a predictive engine constantly generating a "World Model" based on physics, geometry, and social dynamics (the non-linguistic layer).

The Language Layer: Language acts as the control signal for this simulation.

Example: If I say, "Imagine a blue elephant jumping over a fence," your language center parses the syntax and sends a top-down command to your visual cortex to construct that scene.

In a breakup, this is why "talking it out" (linguistic) helps process emotion (non-linguistic). You are using the linguistic OS to structure, bound, and make sense of raw, high-dimensional emotional data that otherwise feels overwhelming.

Language allows us to decouple from the immediate sensory stream, providing the stable tokens required to hold that future goal in place against the wash of immediate sensory data.

In Vygotsky’s theory, mediation is the central process where humans use tools and signs (especially language), provided by their culture, to transform basic mental functions into complex, higher-order thinking

Does feedback-related brain response during reinforcement learning predict socio-motivational (in-)dependence in adolescence?

The role of language in human and machine intelligence

Another modern angle asks what reasoning is for evolutionarily. Mercier and Sperber’s "argumentative theory of reasoning" claims its primary adaptive function isn’t solitary truth-seeking but producing and evaluating arguments in a social context-justifying one’s actions, persuading others, and guarding against being misled. This helps explain why reasoning alone is so prone to confirmation bias and motivated reasoning, yet small groups engaged in critical discussion can be surprisingly good at solving logic and inference tasks. On this picture, the development of reasoning is also the development of argumentation skills and epistemic norms-learning to give reasons, challenge others, handle disagreement, and use language and external notations (diagrams, equations, experiments) as scaffolds. Education then shows up not just as "adding content" but as installing socially shared procedures for how to reason.

The hot/cold distinction is not purely biological; cultural and environmental factors modulate the landscape. Cultures differ in how much they scaffold adolescent decision-making (supervision, structured environments, graduated autonomy) versus allowing autonomous hot-context exposure. They also differ in norms around emotional expression, reward structures for risk-taking, and the social and material consequences of failure. An adolescent in a tightly supervised environment with strong recovery support and tolerance for mistakes may rationally take exploratory risks that would be maladaptive for an adolescent facing permanent consequences for failure (criminal records, loss of educational opportunity, reputational damage in small communities). The developmental question is not just "how robust is hot EF?" but "how well calibrated is hot EF to the actual contingencies of the environment?"–and environments differ enormously in their forgiveness.

Pitfalls

Imitation without understanding; overimitation

The double-edged sword of pedagogy; direct instruction can speed learning but reduce spontaneous exploration and discovery. So a good curriculum for AGI is often interleaved: phases of unguided play/exploration to build broad affordance models, followed by short bursts of instruction/demos that compress the hypothesis space, followed again by play to re-expand and test

Language fundamentally shapes our cognition + allows us to communicate with other agents. In our situation, it is probably necessary for the development of higher-order cognition.

How instruction, joint attention, and cultural transmission massively compress search by providing shaped targets and curricula

Instruction, joint attention, and imitation act like strong priors and KL regularizers that compress search, with language serving as a high-bandwidth index into shared schemas

Learning with language

Language/culture as inductive biases

Humans have the privileged capacity to perceive and act upon shared symbolic (linguistic) spaces 12, 13

Undoubtedly enables efficient communication of culture and concepts (both atomic concepts and the structure of conceptual networks which is encoded in language structure) between agents

Linguistic and physical sensorimotor experiences are fundamentally entangled and cooperative modes of learning and representation 14, 12, 15, 16; linguistic patterns are compact representations of the physical world while sensorimotor patterns act as the ultimate source of linguistic patterns and knowledge in general. They are representing the same universe of patterns but differ in information density and precision; language often trades specificity for efficiency while sensorimotor learning often does the opposite

Desirable properties of language

Discrete, compositional structures

Recursive hierarchies

Role-filler independence

A less obvious benefit of our linguistic capacity is that resulting from the grammatical and amodal structure of languages

Information learned through linguistic communication use allows language to serve as a cognitive "scaffold" for nonlinguistic, semantic cognition 17, expanding our knowledge bases while generally enhancing our ability to relate and compose concepts, or, as Dove puts it, generally enhancing our "cognitive reach". Languages act as a sort of operating system for individual brains, providing abstractions for organizing and accessing knowledge.

Language facilitates intermodal connectivity thanks to the coordination of modalities required by linguistic learning and action

Capacity for language may enhance capacity for fine-grained categorization; evidence from aphasia patients 18, 19, 20; implies that atomic semantic representations are incentivized by the atomic structure of language, allowing humans to quickly latch onto defining characteristics of stimuli

Language is particularly beneficial for learning abstract concepts

Measures of abstraction: degree of appeal to the senses, relational vs individual, context specificity, potential for body-object interaction, etc

These measures directly imply that abstract concepts are more often encountered and more readily processed given linguistic capacity; abstract patterns acquire embodiment through the communication of distributional-linguistic and low-level sensory regions of the brain 16

Discrete conceptual labels present in languages particularly benefit abstract concept learning 21; labels anchor and index categories with highly variable members 16

In line with "cognitive reach" quote; language may allow us to reach higher levels of the conceptual hierarchy

In brains, abstract concepts are stored adjacent to and interact preferentially with linguistic regions

The nature and extent of the influence of language on cognition remains controversial

Semantic memory literature is most likely biased towards the benefits of language, since studies most often use language as a window into semantic memory systems

External scaffolding

Imitation learning

Things learned through imitation must be stamped in through on-policy RL/SSL, no matter the domain; internal inconsistencies must be "wrung out" through rollouts

Mirror neurons

In the premotor and parietal cortices, neurons have been found that fire not only when an individual executes an action, but also when they observe someone else performing that same action. These aptly named mirror neurons (originally discovered in macaques) provide a clear example of embodied representation: the observer’s brain activates its own motor representation of the action as if simulating it

This mirroring mechanism is thought to underlie action understanding and imitation - the brain makes sense of others’ actions by referencing its own motor programs. In humans, brain imaging confirms a similar mirror system engaged during action observation (e.g. watching someone kick a ball engages one’s own motor cortex for leg movements). Such findings support theories of embodied cognition in social contexts: understanding others’ behaviors and intentions is grounded in one’s own embodied action representations
